sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Security vulnerabilities in production code are never forgiven — interviewers assess whether you can reason about authentication and authorisation correctly before trusting you with user data. Freshers are expected to know the authentication vs authorisation distinction, why plain-text passwords are unacceptable, and how JWT tokens work end-to-end. Spring Security's filter chain is a frequent interview topic because it explains how security integrates with every HTTP request.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **Authentication** = proving identity (who are you?) — username + password, token, biometric
- **Authorization** = checking permission (what can you do?) — role checks, scope checks
- **SecurityFilterChain** = an ordered list of servlet filters; every HTTP request passes through them before reaching the controller
- **SecurityContextHolder** = thread-local storage for the current user's authentication object during a request
- **JWT** = three Base64-encoded parts separated by dots: header.payload.signature — stateless and self-contained
- **BCrypt** = adaptive hashing algorithm with work factor; each hash includes a unique salt — never reversible
- **SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS** = tells Spring Security not to create or use HTTP sessions — required for JWT-based APIs
- **@PreAuthorize** = method-level security annotation; evaluated before the method executes using SpEL expressions
- **ROLE_ prefix** = Spring Security's hasRole('ADMIN') automatically prepends ROLE_, while hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN') does not

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- `authentication-vs-authorization` — drill: auth vs authz in one sentence each; principal; granted authority; ROLE_ prefix convention
- `spring-security-filter-chain` — drill: filter chain concept, OncePerRequestFilter, SecurityContextHolder thread-local, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter position
- `jwt-structure-and-flow` — drill: header.payload.signature structure, what each section contains, how the server validates without storing state
- `stateless-vs-stateful-auth` — drill: session-based requires server memory (JSESSIONID cookie) vs JWT stored client-side; REST APIs should be stateless
- `password-encoding-bcrypt` — drill: BCrypt is one-way hash with salt; PasswordEncoder interface; NEVER store plain text or reversible encryption
- `security-configuration-basics` — drill: SecurityFilterChain @Bean, authorizeHttpRequests, permitAll vs authenticated, CORS and CSRF in REST APIs
- `role-based-access-control` — drill: @PreAuthorize uses SpEL, @EnableMethodSecurity activates it, hasRole vs hasAuthority ROLE_ prefix
- `comparisons` — drill: JWT vs session, HS256 (symmetric) vs RS256 (asymmetric), httpBasic vs Bearer token
- `scenario-based` — drill: configure CORS in security, add custom JWT filter, return 401 vs 403 correctly

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "What is the difference between authentication and authorization?" → Authentication = who you are; Authorization = what you're allowed to do
- "Why do we hash passwords with BCrypt instead of encrypting them?" → Encryption is reversible; hashing is one-way — even if the DB is stolen, passwords cannot be recovered
- "What are the three parts of a JWT?" → Header (alg + type), Payload (claims: sub, iat, exp, roles), Signature (HMAC of header.payload)
- "How does the server validate a JWT without hitting the database?" → It re-computes the signature using the secret key and compares; the claims are trusted if the signature matches
- "What is SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS and why is it used with JWT?" → Tells Spring Security not to create HTTP sessions — every request must carry its own authentication token

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In my Spring Boot projects I implement security by configuring a SecurityFilterChain bean. For REST APIs I use JWT — the client authenticates once, receives a signed token, and includes it in the Authorization header on subsequent requests. The server validates the JWT signature and extracts the user's roles from the claims without touching the database. I hash passwords with BCryptPasswordEncoder because BCrypt is a one-way function with a built-in salt — even if someone gets the hash, they cannot recover the password. For endpoint access control I use @PreAuthorize annotations with hasRole() expressions on service methods."*
